@deprecated.summary: @deprecated marks a GraphQL field or enum value as obsolete while keeping it available to clients. Its optional reason tells users what to use instead.
@deprecated.explanation: Place @deprecated on a schema field or enum value to signal that clients should migrate away from it. Its optional reason describes the replacement or rationale; if omitted, the default reason is "No longer supported".
@deprecated.syntax: directive @deprecated(reason: String = "No longer supported") on FIELD_DEFINITION | ENUM_VALUE

parameters.name: reason
parameters.description: Optional explanation of the deprecation and recommended migration; defaults to "No longer supported".

example.title: Deprecate a field
example.explanation: The schema keeps name available while directing clients toward fullName.

useCases.title: Guide clients to a replacement
useCases.scenario: A field has a replacement with a different name or shape.

useCases.title: Retire an enum value safely
useCases.scenario: An enum member should remain readable for existing clients during migration.

useCases.title: Stage a schema migration
useCases.scenario: A schema change must be introduced without immediately breaking existing queries.

interview.question: What does @deprecated do?
interview.answer: @deprecated marks a field or enum value as deprecated without immediately removing it. In SDL implementations, its reason argument defaults to "No longer supported".
interview.followUp: Where can it be applied? The documented locations are FIELD_DEFINITION and ENUM_VALUE.

interview.question: What is the directive signature?
interview.answer: Its declaration accepts an optional String reason and limits use to schema field definitions and enum values. The reason can explain what clients should use instead.
interview.followUp: What happens when reason is omitted? The directive supplies the default text "No longer supported".

interview.question: Why deprecate instead of removing a field immediately?
interview.answer: A deprecated field remains part of the schema, but tools can use the deprecation metadata to guide clients toward a replacement. This supports evolving a schema without an immediate breaking removal.
interview.followUp: How should a replacement be represented? Add the new field, then mark the old field with a reason naming the replacement.

keyPoints: Directives attach metadata or behavior to schema elements; @deprecated communicates that an element should no longer be used.
@deprecated is one of GraphQL's built-in directives.
Its SDL declaration takes an optional String reason and permits placement on field definitions or enum values.
A reason should identify the migration target or recommended replacement.
Development tools can surface deprecation warnings to client authors.
gotchas: The reason argument is nullable and accepts a String; provide a useful migration instruction rather than relying on the default.

@include.summary: @include conditionally includes a field or fragment when its required if argument evaluates to true. Use it to let runtime variables control whether optional selections are requested.
@include.explanation: @include conditionally selects a field, fragment spread, or inline fragment during query execution. Its required Boolean argument controls inclusion: the selection is included when the argument evaluates to true and omitted otherwise.
@include.syntax: directive @include(if: Boolean!) on FIELD | FRAGMENT_SPREAD | INLINE_FRAGMENT

parameters.name: if
parameters.description: Controls whether the annotated selection is included; it must evaluate to true for inclusion.

@include.returns: No standalone value; it controls whether the annotated field or fragment selection contributes to the query result.

example.title: Conditionally include a fragment
example.explanation: The fragment is included in the response only when showDetails is true.

useCases.title: Feature-dependent fields
useCases.scenario: Request optional fields only when a client feature or display mode needs them.

useCases.title: Conditional fragment spreads
useCases.scenario: Enable or omit a reusable group of selections with one runtime Boolean.

useCases.title: Conditional type selections
useCases.scenario: Choose whether type-specific selections are requested in an inline fragment.

interview.question: What does @include do?
interview.answer: @include conditionally includes a field or fragment based on its if argument. The selection is executed only when that argument evaluates to true.
interview.followUp: Where can it be applied? It is valid on fields, fragment spreads, and inline fragments.

interview.question: What is the signature of @include?
interview.answer: The directive takes a required Boolean argument: @include(if: Boolean!). A variable is commonly used so the client can choose the selection at runtime.
interview.followUp: Why is the exclamation mark significant? It makes the argument non-null, so the operation must provide a Boolean value rather than null.

interview.question: How does @include interact with @skip?
interview.answer: With both directives, the selection is included only when @skip is false and @include is true. Neither directive overrides the other.
interview.followUp: What happens if @skip is true? The selection is omitted even when @include is true.

keyPoints: A field annotated with @include appears in the response only when its if argument evaluates to true.
Clients attach @include to fields or fragment inclusions in an executable operation.
@include is one of GraphQL's two built-in executable directives; the other is @skip.
Spec-compliant GraphQL servers provide these built-in directives without requiring custom schema definitions.
gotchas: When both directives are present, inclusion requires @include to be true and @skip to be false; either opposing condition omits the selection.
@include is a built-in directive that compliant GraphQL servers must support, alongside @skip.

@skip.summary: @skip conditionally omits a field or fragment when its Boolean if argument is true. It lets one query make optional selections controlled by a literal or runtime variable.
@skip.explanation: The built-in @skip directive conditionally excludes a field or fragment from query execution when its Boolean if argument is true. Clients can provide a literal or variable value, allowing one operation to request optional data without defining separate queries.

parameters.name: if
parameters.description: Boolean condition that determines whether the annotated field is skipped.

@skip.returns: No value is returned by the directive itself; it controls whether the annotated selection contributes to query execution and results.

example.title: Conditionally skip a field
example.explanation: The variable controls whether the bio field is omitted from execution.

useCases.title: Toggle optional fields
useCases.scenario: A client needs optional profile data without maintaining separate query documents.

useCases.title: Feature-gated selections
useCases.scenario: A feature flag determines whether experimental data should be requested.

useCases.title: Conditionally include fragment data
useCases.scenario: A fragment contains data relevant only for a particular runtime condition.

interview.question: What does @skip do?
interview.answer: @skip conditionally omits a field when its if argument evaluates to true. It is one of the two built-in executable directives that spec-compliant GraphQL servers must support.
interview.followUp: How would you request the field only when a condition is true? Use @include(if: condition), which has the opposite inclusion behavior.

interview.question: How is the skip condition supplied?
interview.answer: The directive takes a Boolean if argument and can be attached to a field or fragment inclusion. A variable is useful when the condition is supplied at runtime.
interview.followUp: What happens when the variable is true? The annotated selection is skipped, so it is not included in the response data.

interview.question: Show a practical client query using @skip.
interview.answer: A client can place @skip on a field, such as bio, and pass a Boolean variable in the operation variables. The server then evaluates that condition during execution.
interview.followUp: Why use this instead of separate query documents? It keeps one operation reusable while allowing optional selections to be controlled by runtime input.

keyPoints: @skip applies to an individual field or to a fragment inclusion in an executable operation.
Its companion @include directive expresses the inverse condition: include a selection only when the Boolean is true.
The selection is skipped whenever the directive's Boolean argument is true.
Portable GraphQL clients can rely on these directives when communicating with specification-compliant servers.
gotchas: A true if value omits the selected field or fragment from the result.
@skip is a standard built-in directive, but a server must support it as part of GraphQL specification compliance.

@specifiedBy.summary: @specifiedBy documents a custom scalar by attaching a URL for its specification. The URL should explain the scalar’s format, serialization, and coercion rules.
@specifiedBy.explanation: Apply @specifiedBy to a custom scalar in SDL to publish the URL of its human-readable specification. That document should define the scalar’s data format, serialization, and coercion rules so compatible tools and systems can understand its behavior.

parameters.name: url
parameters.description: URL of the custom scalar’s human-readable specification.

example.title: Specify a UUID scalar
example.code: scalar UUID @specifiedBy(url: "https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc4122")
example.explanation: Declares a custom UUID scalar and associates it with a human-readable specification URL.

useCases.title: Document a UUID scalar
useCases.scenario: A service defines a UUID scalar and wants clients to discover the UUID rules.

useCases.title: Publish custom format rules
useCases.scenario: A team publishes a custom date-time format and needs to associate that contract with its scalar.

useCases.title: Support schema introspection
useCases.scenario: Schema tooling exposes scalar metadata through introspection.

interview.question: What is @specifiedBy used for?
interview.answer: @specifiedBy is a built-in type-system directive for documenting a custom scalar. Its required url argument identifies the scalar’s specification, and the directive can be introspected.
interview.followUp: What should the target document contain? It should be human-readable and define the scalar’s format, serialization, and coercion rules.

interview.question: What is the directive’s signature and location?
interview.answer: Its SDL signature is `directive @specifiedBy(url: String!) on SCALAR`. Therefore, it accepts one required non-null String argument and can be applied only to scalar definitions.
interview.followUp: Can it annotate a field? No. Its location is SCALAR, so it describes the scalar type rather than an individual field use.

interview.question: Why does the URL matter to clients and tools?
interview.answer: A service should provide a specification URL when defining a custom scalar. Tools aware of that URL can use the documented rules to conform to the scalar’s behavior.
interview.followUp: What should happen when no URL is supplied? The directive is not required for every scalar by the signature, but a service should provide one for a custom scalar specification.

keyPoints: It is a built-in SDL directive for documenting scalar behavior.
A custom scalar can publish its specification URL through this directive.
The referenced document must be readable by people, not just machine-oriented metadata.
Compatible systems should follow the rules described by the linked specification.
gotchas: Do not attach the directive to built-in scalars such as String, Int, Float, Boolean, or ID.
The URL should describe the scalar’s format and conversion rules, not merely point to an arbitrary page.

ApolloServer.summary: ApolloServer is Apollo’s JavaScript GraphQL server. Construct it with schema definitions and resolvers, then run it standalone or connect it to a Node.js HTTP framework.
ApolloServer.explanation: ApolloServer creates a GraphQL server from a schema definition and resolver map. The standalone starter attaches it to a built-in HTTP server; integrations are also available for Node.js frameworks and serverless environments.

parameters.name: typeDefs
parameters.description: GraphQL schema written as a schema definition string.

parameters.name: resolvers
parameters.description: Map of resolver functions that return field data.

ApolloServer.returns: An ApolloServer instance that can be started with a standalone server or connected through a framework integration.

example.title: Minimal Apollo Server
example.explanation: Defines a schema and resolver, creates Apollo Server with them, and starts its standalone HTTP server.

useCases.title: Standalone GraphQL service
useCases.scenario: Building a small Node.js GraphQL API without selecting an HTTP framework.

useCases.title: Framework integration
useCases.scenario: Embedding GraphQL in an existing Node.js web application.

useCases.title: Performance and security features
useCases.scenario: Improving API operations and protection.

interview.question: What inputs does ApolloServer need to serve a GraphQL API?
interview.answer: ApolloServer is constructed with schema definitions and resolvers. The schema describes the available GraphQL operations, while resolvers provide the functions that return field data.
interview.followUp: How would you adapt it to an existing web application? Use Apollo Server's framework integration API instead of relying on the built-in standalone HTTP server.

interview.question: How do you start an Apollo Server instance?
interview.answer: After construction, the server can be passed to startStandaloneServer, which starts Apollo Server's built-in HTTP server and returns its URL. The server can also work with Node.js HTTP frameworks through integrations.
interview.followUp: What additional capabilities are documented? Apollo Server provides a plugin API, Apollo Studio integration, caching, automatic persisted queries, and CSRF prevention.

interview.question: What ecosystem does Apollo Server target?
interview.answer: Apollo Server is a JavaScript GraphQL server that works with any Node.js HTTP framework. Its basic setup uses the @apollo/server package together with graphql.
interview.followUp: What does the standalone example demonstrate? It installs both packages, declares a Query type, supplies a resolver, constructs ApolloServer, and starts the server.

keyPoints: Apollo Server is a JavaScript GraphQL server designed to run with Node.js HTTP frameworks.
Its setup begins by declaring the GraphQL schema, such as a Query type and its fields.
Resolvers are supplied as a map of functions that produce values for schema fields.
Create the server by passing the schema definitions and resolver map to the ApolloServer constructor.
The platform exposes a plugin API for extending server behavior.
Documented operational features include caching, automatic persisted queries, and CSRF prevention.
gotchas: The standalone starter is convenient for a basic server, but applications using other HTTP frameworks or serverless environments should use an appropriate integration.

assertValidSchema.summary: A GraphQL schema describes the data an API exposes and the relationships between that data. Its type system helps clients write valid queries with predictable results.
assertValidSchema.explanation: The GraphQL schema describes every kind of data that an API can return and how those data types are related. It uses named types such as object, scalar, and enum types, plus list and non-null modifiers, so clients can form queries with predictable results.

example.title: A small GraphQL schema
example.explanation: This schema defines a query field named `user`. The field returns a `User` object with a required ID and an optional name.

useCases.title: Describe available data
useCases.scenario: Designing an API contract

useCases.title: Discover queryable fields
useCases.scenario: Building a client

useCases.title: Catch invalid queries early
useCases.scenario: Checking operations before execution

interview.question: What is a GraphQL schema?
interview.answer: A schema is the contract that describes the data an API exposes and the relationships between that data. Clients use it to create queries whose result shape can be predicted.
interview.followUp: How does a server check a query before running it? It parses the document first, then validates it against the schema’s type system.

interview.question: Which kinds of types can a GraphQL schema define?
interview.answer: Named types describe the API’s data model. GraphQL supports object, scalar, enum, input object, interface, and union type definitions.
interview.followUp: What do list and non-null types do? They wrap another type: a list describes multiple values, while non-null says a value cannot be null.

interview.question: Why is schema validation useful?
interview.answer: Validation checks an operation against the schema before execution. This lets the server report invalid queries early instead of discovering those problems during runtime checks.
interview.followUp: What happens after validation succeeds? The server can execute the operation and return its result.

keyPoints: The type system defines which data clients may query.
A schema is the complete set of capabilities exposed by a GraphQL service.
The six named definitions are object, scalar, enum, input object, interface, and union types.
Clients use the schema to shape queries and anticipate the returned data.
A server parses an operation before checking it against the schema.
gotchas: A query can have valid GraphQL syntax but still fail validation if it does not match the schema.

buildASTSchema.summary: buildASTSchema builds a GraphQL schema from a parsed schema definition document. The schema describes the data and operations that clients can query.
buildASTSchema.explanation: buildASTSchema creates a GraphQLSchema object from a parsed GraphQL schema definition language document. The resulting object describes the API types and fields, so GraphQL tools can inspect and use the schema.

parameters.name: ast
parameters.description: A parsed GraphQL schema definition language document containing the type definitions used to build the schema.

buildASTSchema.returns: A GraphQLSchema object built from the schema definition document.

example.title: Build a schema from GraphQL syntax
example.explanation: This builds a GraphQL schema from a parsed schema definition and reads the type of the greeting field.

useCases.title: Build a schema
useCases.scenario: Create a GraphQLSchema object from schema definition language during application startup.

useCases.title: Read API capabilities
useCases.scenario: Inspect available types and fields for tooling or validation.

interview.question: What does buildASTSchema do?
interview.answer: buildASTSchema converts a parsed GraphQL schema definition into a GraphQLSchema object. The input must be an AST, such as the result of parsing GraphQL schema language.
interview.followUp: What happens if the document contains invalid schema definitions? The schema-building step reports validation or construction errors instead of producing a usable schema.

interview.question: Why does a GraphQL API need a schema?
interview.answer: A GraphQL schema defines the data that clients can query. It names types, fields, and relationships, and the schema lets clients form queries with predictable result shapes.
interview.followUp: Why is this different from a query document? A query asks for data, while the schema describes which data and operations the API supports.

interview.question: What kinds of definitions can a schema contain?
interview.answer: The function works with the GraphQL type system, including object types such as Query and scalar field types such as String. A non-null marker, written with !, requires a field value to be present.
interview.followUp: How can a client learn the available types and fields? GraphQL provides introspection, which exposes schema information through queries.

keyPoints: A schema describes the data that an API allows clients to query.
The schema is the complete set of query capabilities offered by the service.
Clients use the schema to write queries with known result shapes.
GraphQL has six named type-definition categories in its type system.

buildSchema.summary: `buildSchema` builds a GraphQL schema from Schema Definition Language (SDL). The resulting schema describes the types and fields that GraphQL operations can validate and execute against.
buildSchema.explanation: `buildSchema` converts a GraphQL schema written in SDL into a `GraphQLSchema` object that can validate and execute operations. Root fields can resolve through the supplied root value; more advanced resolver behavior generally uses explicit schema construction APIs.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: A GraphQL SDL document containing the schema definition.

buildSchema.returns: A GraphQL schema representing the types and fields declared in the SDL.

example.title: Build a schema from SDL
example.explanation: Builds an executable schema from SDL, supplies a resolver through the root value, and executes a query against it.

useCases.title: Schema-first API design
useCases.scenario: Define a service contract in a readable, language-agnostic SDL file before implementing its data resolvers.

useCases.title: Query validation and execution
useCases.scenario: Create the schema object used to validate incoming operations and execute them.

useCases.title: Self-documenting APIs
useCases.scenario: Expose type, field, and argument descriptions for client tooling and schema exploration.

interview.question: What does `buildSchema` create, and what is the resulting object used for?
interview.answer: `buildSchema` takes SDL and produces a schema object representing the service’s supported types and fields. GraphQL then validates and executes incoming operations against that schema.
interview.followUp: Why might a team use explicit schema construction instead? It can keep resolver functions and schema types together, rather than defining the type system separately in SDL.

interview.question: What role does SDL play when using `buildSchema`?
interview.answer: SDL is a language-agnostic way to describe GraphQL types and fields. The resulting schema defines the capabilities that clients can query, while resolver logic supplies field values.
interview.followUp: How can a schema be documented? GraphQL supports descriptions on types, fields, and arguments, including Markdown-formatted descriptions.

interview.question: Why is a schema required in a GraphQL service?
interview.answer: A GraphQL schema describes the possible data available from a service, including its types and fields. Requests are checked against that schema before execution, which makes results predictable.
interview.followUp: What other schema-building approaches exist? Libraries may construct types in code, infer schemas from resolver annotations, or infer both schema and resolvers from data sources.

keyPoints: The SDL supplied to `buildSchema` describes the data shape and capabilities exposed by the API.
A schema covers the complete set of queryable types for the service, not just one operation.
`buildSchema` is useful when you prefer a readable, language-agnostic schema declaration.
Object types declare fetchable entities and the fields available on them.
SDL can include descriptions that make the generated schema easier for clients and developers to understand.
A schema built from SDL can contain the six named type categories defined by GraphQL.
gotchas: The SDL passed to `buildSchema` describes the type system, but it does not by itself provide application data or resolver behavior.
A built schema is used for validation and execution; creating it does not execute a query.

concatAST.summary: GraphQL is a query language for client applications. Clients describe the data they need, and a service returns data through a shared type system and interface.
concatAST.explanation: The GraphQL specification presents a query language for describing the data a client needs. A service exposes its capabilities through GraphQL's common type system, while the service decides how to implement storage and execution.
concatAST.returns: The service returns data shaped by the fields selected in the request.

example.title: Request a user's name
example.explanation: This query asks for one user's name and supplies the user ID as a variable.

useCases.title: Request specific data
useCases.scenario: A client needs only selected fields from a service response.

useCases.title: Share one service interface
useCases.scenario: Several clients use services with different internal implementations.

useCases.title: Build GraphQL tools
useCases.scenario: Development teams need tools built around a described API.

interview.question: What is GraphQL used for?
interview.answer: GraphQL lets a client describe the data it needs in a structured request. The service maps its own capabilities to GraphQL's shared language and type system.
interview.followUp: Does GraphQL require a specific database? No. The specification leaves the storage system to the service implementation.

interview.question: Is GraphQL a general-purpose programming language?
interview.answer: No. GraphQL is a language for making requests to application services. It does not provide arbitrary computation like a general-purpose programming language.
interview.followUp: What does the service do instead? It executes requests using capabilities defined by its GraphQL schema.

interview.question: Does GraphQL prescribe an implementation technology?
interview.answer: No. GraphQL does not require one implementation language or storage system. Each service chooses how to implement its capabilities behind the GraphQL interface.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful? Clients can use a consistent request language even when services use different internal technologies.

keyPoints: GraphQL is intended for client applications that need to describe their data requirements.
Its syntax and system are designed to express data requirements in a flexible way.
Clients send requests to services whose capabilities are described by the GraphQL specification.
A service maps its own capabilities into GraphQL's common language and type system.
The shared interface helps product development work with different application services.
The GraphQL model also supports tools that inspect and work with the service interface.
gotchas: GraphQL describes requests to a service; it is not intended for general-purpose computation.
An implementation can use different programming languages and storage technologies.

context.summary: GraphQL is commonly served through one HTTP endpoint, typically `/graphql`. Clients send JSON requests, usually with POST, and receive results under `data` plus any validation or execution errors under `errors`.
context.explanation: In GraphQL HTTP handling, authentication runs before request validation so resolvers can access session and user information. The request is usually sent as JSON to one service endpoint, with the operation in the body; query operations may also use GET.
context.returns: A JSON-encoded response containing the operation result under `data` and any validation or execution errors under `errors`.

example.title: Send a GraphQL query over HTTP
example.explanation: A client sends a GraphQL query to the service endpoint as a JSON HTTP POST request.

useCases.title: Submit GraphQL operations over HTTP
useCases.scenario: Calling queries or mutations from a web or backend client.

useCases.title: Allow GET for query operations
useCases.scenario: Supporting clients that need cacheable, read-only requests.

useCases.title: Process data and errors from responses
useCases.scenario: Returning predictable machine-readable results and failures.

interview.question: How are GraphQL APIs commonly exposed over HTTP?
interview.answer: GraphQL commonly uses one endpoint, typically `/graphql`, rather than a URL per entity. Requests identify the operation and selection set in the GraphQL document sent to that endpoint.
interview.followUp: Can GraphQL use a transport other than HTTP? Yes. GraphQL is transport-agnostic, although HTTP is the common choice.

interview.question: Which HTTP methods are used for GraphQL operations?
interview.answer: A server must accept POST for query and mutation operations. It may also accept GET for query operations, but GET is not the general-purpose method for mutations.
interview.followUp: What should a client send to indicate the desired response format? It should include `application/graphql-response+json` in the `Accept` header.

interview.question: How are GraphQL HTTP responses and errors represented?
interview.answer: The JSON response places the full or partial successful result under `data`. Validation or execution problems are reported under `errors`; both keys can occur when execution returns partial data.
interview.followUp: Where should authorization be implemented? In the business logic during GraphQL execution, after authentication has established the user context.

keyPoints: GraphQL models connected entities as a graph instead of exposing each entity through a separate resource URL.
A service generally directs all GraphQL requests to one endpoint, commonly named `/graphql`.
JSON is the baseline serialization format clients and servers should support.
Clients should advertise the GraphQL response media type through the Accept header.
Successful results, including partial results, are returned under the data property.
Validation and execution failures are represented in the errors property.
gotchas: Place GraphQL after authentication middleware so the request has access to the same session and user information as other handlers.
Do not treat authentication middleware as the complete authorization layer; enforce authorization while business logic executes.
POST is required for queries and mutations; GET is optional for queries only.
A JSON POST request needs the corresponding Content-Type header.

createSchema.summary: A GraphQL schema defines what data an API exposes and how that data is shaped. Its type system lets clients send valid queries with predictable results.
createSchema.explanation: A GraphQL schema defines the data and operations that an API allows clients to query. Types describe values, fields describe available data, and relationships between types describe how clients can move through the graph.

example.title: Create and query a small schema
example.explanation: This creates a schema with one required field and runs a query against it.

useCases.title: Describe an API contract
useCases.scenario: Define the fields and operations available in an API.

useCases.title: Represent data relationships
useCases.scenario: Model connected data such as users, posts, and comments.

useCases.title: Enable schema-aware clients
useCases.scenario: Support client tools that need to understand available fields and types.

interview.question: What is a GraphQL schema?
interview.answer: A schema is the contract for a GraphQL service. It describes the fields clients may query and the types of values those fields return.
interview.followUp: How does a client discover this contract? GraphQL supports introspection, which lets tools and clients inspect the schema.

interview.question: What is the role of a field type?
interview.answer: A field belongs to an object type and describes one piece of data that can be selected. Its type tells the client what shape the returned value has.
interview.followUp: Why are field types useful? They let clients validate queries and make result shapes predictable before a request runs.

interview.question: Why is GraphQL's type system separate from the backend?
interview.answer: GraphQL types describe the data exposed by an API and the relationships between pieces of data. Because GraphQL can work with different backends and languages, the type system is separate from the implementation.
interview.followUp: Does the schema require a particular database? No. The schema describes the API contract, while resolver or backend code supplies the data.

keyPoints: The type system defines which data a client may request.
A schema is the complete set of capabilities exposed by a service.
Clients use the schema to form valid queries and expect stable result shapes.
GraphQL has six named type-definition categories that describe API data.
Types can model both data and links between related data.
The schema is independent of the backend framework or programming language.
gotchas: A client can query only fields defined by the schema. Unsupported fields fail validation before execution.

DataLoader.sourceTitle: Wrapping a REST API in GraphQL
DataLoader.summary: DataLoader batches keyed data fetches and memoizes repeated keys, helping GraphQL resolvers avoid duplicate backend requests. Create it with a function that maps a list of keys to the corresponding objects.
DataLoader.explanation: DataLoader is a utility for a data-fetching layer that accepts keys, resolves them in batches, and caches repeated lookups. In GraphQL resolvers, load() and loadMany() help avoid repeated backend requests for the same data.

parameters.name: keys
parameters.description: Keys collected for the batch operation; the example uses REST API URLs.

DataLoader.returns: The batch function returns the objects corresponding to the supplied keys; individual load calls return the associated value or Promise.

example.title: Batch and cache person lookups
example.explanation: The loader receives keys, fetches the corresponding people together, and memoizes repeated keys during its lifetime.

useCases.title: Prevent duplicate REST requests
useCases.scenario: Several GraphQL fields need the same remote resource during one operation.

useCases.title: Batch keyed data fetching
useCases.scenario: Many resolver calls request related records from a backend.

useCases.title: Load individual or multiple keys
useCases.scenario: A resolver needs one or several resources through a shared loader.

interview.question: What problem does DataLoader solve?
interview.answer: DataLoader accepts a batch function that resolves a list of objects from a list of keys. It combines requested keys and can memoize results, reducing duplicate backend requests.
interview.followUp: What does the batch function receive? It receives the keys collected by the loader, such as URLs, and returns the corresponding results in the batch.

interview.question: How do callers use a DataLoader instance?
interview.answer: Use load() for one key and loadMany() for multiple keys. Both allow callers to request data without repeatedly contacting the backend for the same key.
interview.followUp: When is memoization useful? It is useful when multiple resolvers request the same resource during the loader's lifetime.

interview.question: What does the DataLoader constructor require?
interview.answer: The constructor receives a function that maps a list of keys to a list of results. For URL-backed data, that function can fetch each URL and combine the resulting promises.
interview.followUp: What runtime features does the implementation rely on? It relies on Promise and Map, supplied natively or by polyfills.

keyPoints: DataLoader is presented as a library for reducing repeated requests caused by GraphQL query execution.
Its constructor takes a batch function whose input is keys and whose output is the associated objects.
Keys can be identifiers for an underlying source; the documented example uses REST endpoint URLs.
Use load() for an individual key and loadMany() when requesting several keys.
Memoization prevents duplicate requests for the same URL through one loader instance.
gotchas: Caching lasts for the loader's lifetime, so create a loader with an appropriate scope rather than assuming it is a permanent cache.
The runtime must provide Promise and Map, either natively or through polyfills.

defaultFieldResolver.summary: defaultFieldResolver is the conventional behavior used by many GraphQL libraries when no field resolver is supplied: read the same-named property from the parent object and return it. It suits simple fields whose values are already present on that object.
defaultFieldResolver.explanation: GraphQL’s default field behavior resolves a field by reading a property with the same name from the parent object when no custom resolver is supplied. This is useful for simple fields whose response value is already present on the parent object.
defaultFieldResolver.returns: The value produced for the field; for a trivial resolver, the same-named property from the parent object.

example.title: Same-name property resolution
example.explanation: A trivial resolver can return a same-named property from the parent object.

useCases.title: Expose stored object properties
useCases.scenario: A parent object already contains a scalar field with the same name as the GraphQL field.

useCases.title: Reduce boilerplate for simple types
useCases.scenario: A type has several straightforward fields that require no computation or data fetching.

useCases.title: Resolve nested object data
useCases.scenario: A nested selection reads fields directly from an object returned by an earlier resolver.

interview.question: What is a resolver, and how does the default behavior work?
interview.answer: A resolver is the function backing a GraphQL field. During execution, GraphQL calls the resolver for the field to produce the next value; for a trivial field, many libraries can instead read a same-named property from the parent object.
interview.followUp: What happens when the field has a custom resolver? The custom resolver is used to compute the field’s value instead of relying on the same-name property convention.

interview.question: When can a resolver be omitted?
interview.answer: A trivial resolver is appropriate when the value is already stored on the parent object under the GraphQL field’s name. In that case, no explicit resolver is needed in libraries that support this convention.
interview.followUp: When should an explicit resolver be preferred? Use one when the value requires computation, arguments, external data access, or a property name different from the schema field.

interview.question: How does a resolved field appear in the GraphQL response?
interview.answer: Field execution produces values that are placed into a response map under the field name or alias. The resolved value then supplies the next part of the result structure.
interview.followUp: What determines the response key? An alias becomes the response key; without an alias, the field name is used.

keyPoints: Each selected field conceptually acts like a function or method on the value produced by the preceding field.
GraphQL servers associate fields with resolver behavior that produces their values.
Execution invokes the field’s resolver to obtain the value used for the next stage.
The trivial-resolver convention reads and returns a parent property whose name matches the field.
Resolved values are stored in the response map using the field name or its alias as the key.
gotchas: This behavior is a library convention rather than a universal GraphQL specification requirement; verify how the server library implements omitted resolvers.

directive.summary: A GraphQL directive is an `@` annotation that changes how a schema or operation is interpreted. Directives may annotate schema definitions, affect client operations, and are restricted to declared locations.
directive.explanation: A GraphQL directive is an annotation beginning with `@` that can alter how a schema element or operation is validated or executed. Executable directives can be placed in client operations, while type-system directives annotate schema definitions; each directive declares the locations where it is allowed.

parameters.name: if
parameters.description: For the built-in executable directives, a Boolean condition named `if` controls inclusion or skipping.

directive.returns: Directives do not return a standalone value; they influence validation, schema interpretation, or operation execution.

example.title: Conditionally include a field
example.explanation: The variable controls whether the email field is included in the response.

useCases.title: Conditional query fields
useCases.scenario: Omit optional fields based on a client-provided Boolean.

useCases.title: Schema annotation
useCases.scenario: Mark schema elements for special validation or execution treatment.

useCases.title: Custom directives
useCases.scenario: Apply reusable application-specific behavior beyond ordinary field arguments.

interview.question: What is a GraphQL directive?
interview.answer: Directives are `@` annotations that can change validation or execution behavior. They can be attached to schema definitions as type-system directives or used in operations as executable directives.
interview.followUp: How does a client conditionally omit a field? Use `@include(if: Boolean)` and provide a Boolean value; use `@skip(if: Boolean)` when the field should be excluded when the value is true.

interview.question: Which built-in directives should a compliant server support?
interview.answer: The built-in executable directives are `@include(if: Boolean)` and `@skip(if: Boolean)`. The former includes a field only when its argument is true, while the latter skips it when its argument is true.
interview.followUp: Where can these directives be attached? They can be used on fields and fragment inclusion, according to the queries documentation.

interview.question: How are custom directives constrained?
interview.answer: A custom directive must be defined with its allowed locations, such as `FIELD_DEFINITION` or `ENUM_VALUE`. Its use is then restricted to those declared locations.
interview.followUp: Why use a custom directive? It can encode reusable schema annotation or operation behavior when ordinary field arguments are insufficient.

keyPoints: The `@` prefix identifies a directive and signals that it may modify a schema or operation.
Type-system directives annotate schema types, fields, and arguments for different validation or execution treatment.
Executable directives are designed for placement in client operations rather than only in schema definitions.
A directive definition must declare its permitted locations, which determines where clients or schema authors may apply it.
GraphQL supports application-specific directives in addition to the directives supplied by the core language.
gotchas: A client cannot assume that a custom directive exists: the target server must support the directive used by the operation.

enum.summary: GraphQL enums are scalar-like leaf types constrained to a finite set of named values. They validate enum arguments and describe the possible values a field can return.
enum.explanation: An enum is a leaf type whose values are limited to a finite, explicitly declared set. The schema uses an enum declaration to define those values, and clients use the unquoted names wherever that enum type is expected.
enum.returns: A named value from the enum's declared finite set.

example.title: Defining and using an enum
example.explanation: The schema defines the allowed episode values, and the query supplies one enum value without quotes.

useCases.title: Constrain domain values
useCases.scenario: Model a field with a small, closed set of valid outcomes such as an episode, status, or category.

useCases.title: Validate inputs
useCases.scenario: Expose valid argument choices directly through the schema so invalid names are rejected during validation.

useCases.title: Describe output contracts
useCases.scenario: Help clients understand the finite set of values a field may return.

interview.question: What is a GraphQL enum, and why use one?
interview.answer: An enum is a special scalar restricted to a defined set of values. It communicates that a field can produce only one member of that finite set and lets GraphQL validate enum arguments.
interview.followUp: What kind of value does an enum represent internally? The documentation distinguishes enum values from numeric references: they are unique values that may serialize using their names.

interview.question: How are enum values written in a query?
interview.answer: Enum values are written as unquoted names because the expected enum type is already known from the schema. For example, a query can pass JEDI rather than the string "JEDI".
interview.followUp: Why is the enum type name omitted at the use site? The surrounding argument or field type supplies the precise enumeration context.

interview.question: How do enums participate in query execution?
interview.answer: Enums are leaf values, so GraphQL queries end when they reach an enum field; clients do not select subfields from an enum. The server must return one of the values declared for that enum.
interview.followUp: How can a server map an enum to internal data? Execution can coerce an internal representation, such as a number, into the schema's expected enum value.

keyPoints: Enums belong to the scalar category, but unlike ordinary scalars they constrain values to named members.
Every enum declaration establishes the complete set of values accepted for that type.
Enum-typed arguments receive schema validation against the declared members.
A field's enum type tells clients which finite outcomes the field may expose.
Enum fields terminate selections and cannot contain nested field selections.
The enum's declaration controls the legal values everywhere that enum type is referenced.

execute.summary: GraphQL execution runs a parsed and validated operation against a schema. It resolves requested fields, completes their values, and returns data shaped like the client’s operation, potentially with errors.
execute.explanation: Execution runs a validated GraphQL operation against an existing schema. It starts at the root Query, Mutation, or Subscription fields, invokes resolvers for requested fields, completes nested selections or scalar values, and produces a response that mirrors the query shape; resolvers can perform asynchronous work.
execute.returns: A GraphQL response whose data mirrors the requested operation; it may also include errors and extensions.

example.title: Executing a GraphQL operation
example.explanation: A server executes the parsed and validated operation against its schema and returns data shaped like the request.

useCases.title: Query execution
useCases.scenario: Run a read operation against a GraphQL schema and return the requested fields.

useCases.title: Mutation execution
useCases.scenario: Apply server-side state changes through a mutation's root fields.

useCases.title: Subscription execution
useCases.scenario: Resolve event-driven subscription operations and produce results for events.

useCases.title: Shape-preserving responses
useCases.scenario: Assemble nested response objects whose keys match fields or aliases in the operation.

interview.question: How does GraphQL execution produce a response?
interview.answer: Execution begins with the operation's root type: Query, Mutation, or Subscription. The executor resolves requested fields, recursively completes object selections, and coerces leaf values to the schema's expected types.
interview.followUp: How can a response contain both data and errors? A field resolver may fail after other fields have resolved, allowing partial data while the failure is reported in errors.

interview.question: What role do field resolvers play during execution?
interview.answer: Each requested field is backed by a resolver. The resolver receives the relevant parent value and produces the next value; that value is then completed either by running a nested selection set or by coercing a scalar.
interview.followUp: What happens for an asynchronous resolver? Execution can await asynchronous resolver results before completing the field and assembling the response.

interview.question: How is the response shape determined?
interview.answer: The result is assembled as a key-value map while fields resolve. A field name, or its alias when one is present, becomes the key, so the returned structure mirrors the client's requested shape.
interview.followUp: Why are aliases significant? They let multiple selections use distinct response keys even when they refer to fields with the same underlying name.

keyPoints: Execution follows parsing and validation; the server runs only after the document passes those earlier phases.
The operation type selects the root object from which field resolution starts.
Resolvers are the server-defined functions that supply values for schema fields.
Resolver implementations may perform asynchronous work, so execution supports asynchronous data retrieval.
Leaf results are coerced to the schema's declared scalar types before they are returned.
Response keys come from field names or aliases, preserving the requested response structure.

extendSchema.summary: GraphQL is a query language for client applications. Clients describe the fields they need, and an application service returns data in that requested shape.
extendSchema.explanation: A GraphQL client sends a query that describes the fields it needs. The application service maps its own data and capabilities to GraphQL's common language and type system, then returns data that follows the requested field shape. GraphQL does not require a specific programming language or storage system.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The user identifier supplied to the query.

extendSchema.returns: An object containing the requested user name.

example.title: Fetch a user's name
example.explanation: This query asks for the name of one user. The variable supplies the user ID at runtime.

useCases.title: Request view data
useCases.scenario: A screen needs a user's name and other profile fields.

useCases.title: Unify application data
useCases.scenario: A team needs one API interface over different data stores.

useCases.title: Build developer tools
useCases.scenario: Tools need to inspect available fields and types.

interview.question: What is GraphQL?
interview.answer: GraphQL is a query language for describing data requirements and interactions. A client requests fields, and the service returns data in the requested structure.
interview.followUp: Does GraphQL require a specific database? No. The specification does not require a particular programming language or storage system.

interview.question: How does a GraphQL request work?
interview.answer: A GraphQL operation names the fields the client needs, such as a user's name. The service maps those fields to its own underlying data sources and returns the matching result.
interview.followUp: What controls the available fields? The service exposes capabilities through its GraphQL schema and type system.

interview.question: Why use a GraphQL interface?
interview.answer: GraphQL gives clients a uniform language and type system while leaving implementation choices to the application service. This makes the interface consistent even when the underlying systems differ.
interview.followUp: What does GraphQL not define? It does not define a required programming language, storage system, or arbitrary-computation model.

keyPoints: GraphQL lets client applications describe the data they need with a query language.
Its syntax describes data requirements and interactions in a structured way.
A service maps its own capabilities into GraphQL's uniform language.
GraphQL also provides a shared type system and set of design ideas.
Implementations may choose their programming language and storage system.
The result is one interface that client and product teams can use consistently.
gotchas: GraphQL cannot perform arbitrary computations like a general-purpose programming language. It is used to request data from an application service.

federation.summary: GraphQL federation combines independently managed subgraphs into one schema exposed through a gateway. Clients query the unified schema while the gateway routes work to the responsible services.
federation.explanation: Federation divides a GraphQL API across independently managed subgraphs. A gateway composes their schemas into one schema for clients, routes query portions to the relevant services, gathers the results, and returns one response.
federation.returns: A unified GraphQL schema and, at runtime, a single response assembled from results returned by the relevant subgraphs.

example.explanation: A subgraph can define a product entity using a key field so the gateway can connect it with related data from other subgraphs.

useCases.title: Let teams own and deploy domain-specific subgraphs independently.
useCases.scenario: Large organizations

useCases.title: Present many services through one consistent GraphQL entry point.
useCases.scenario: Microservice architectures

useCases.title: Assemble data from multiple services into one client response.
useCases.scenario: Cross-domain queries

useCases.title: Use composition and a registry to validate relationships and compatibility.
useCases.scenario: Schema governance

interview.question: What is GraphQL federation?
interview.answer: Federation organizes a GraphQL API as multiple independent subgraphs, each owning part of the data graph. A gateway composes those schemas into a unified schema that clients query.
interview.followUp: What happens when a client query spans services? The gateway divides the work among the appropriate subgraphs, collects their results, and assembles one response.

interview.question: What are the main components of a federated GraphQL system?
interview.answer: A subgraph is an individual service with its own GraphQL schema and resolvers. Schema composition combines subgraph schemas and resolves the relationships between them.
interview.followUp: Why is composition necessary? It detects incompatibilities and ensures types are connected correctly before the gateway exposes the combined schema.

interview.question: How would you introduce federation into an existing system?
interview.answer: Start by defining service boundaries, designing schemas around those boundaries, implementing the subgraphs, and deploying a gateway. A schema registry can manage composition and validation.
interview.followUp: What operational concern does a registry address? It helps verify schema integrity as independently deployed subgraphs change.

keyPoints: Federation lets independently managed services collaborate without requiring them to become one deployable application.
Clients see one GraphQL schema even though its fields are implemented by multiple subgraphs.
A subgraph should own a coherent domain or portion of the overall data graph.
The gateway is the central entry point that coordinates composition and distributed query execution.
Composition merges subgraph definitions into the schema exposed to clients.
A query spanning domains is split and routed to the services responsible for its requested data.
gotchas: The gateway is a runtime coordinator, so it must be deployed and operated as an additional service between clients and subgraphs.

field resolver.summary: A field resolver is the server function that supplies a value for a GraphQL field. GraphQL calls resolvers from the root operation fields through nested selections until the requested leaf values are produced.
field resolver.explanation: A field resolver is the server-side function associated with a schema field. GraphQL calls it during execution, starting from root operation fields and continuing through nested selections; the returned value is then completed according to the field's type. Resolvers can use the parent object, field arguments, shared context, and execution metadata.

parameters.description: The previous object; commonly unused for a field on the root Query type.

parameters.name: args
parameters.description: Arguments supplied to the field in the GraphQL operation.

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: Shared value available to every resolver, such as the authenticated user or a database handle.

parameters.name: info
parameters.description: Field-specific information about the current operation and schema; generally for advanced use cases.

field resolver.returns: A value for the field's declared type; object values are recursively completed through their selected subfields, while scalar values complete at the leaf.

example.title: Resolvers for two fields
example.explanation: Each resolver receives the parent value and can obtain data from request context or another data source.

useCases.title: Resolve root fields
useCases.scenario: Fetch a root resource such as the current user from request authentication context.

useCases.title: Resolve nested fields
useCases.scenario: Use the parent object's identifier to retrieve a related property from a database or repository.

useCases.title: Use request context
useCases.scenario: Access authentication details, database handles, or other request-scoped services shared through context.

useCases.title: Resolve asynchronously
useCases.scenario: Return data from a remote or database-backed source that requires awaiting asynchronous work.

interview.question: What is a GraphQL field resolver?
interview.answer: A resolver is the function that supplies a field's value. GraphQL invokes it when executing that field, and nested object results lead to execution of their selected subfields.
interview.followUp: What are the resolver arguments? The reference implementation passes the previous object, field arguments, shared context, and field-specific execution information.

interview.question: What does the parent argument contain?
interview.answer: The first argument is the previous object, often called the parent value. For a root Query field it is commonly unused; for a nested field it represents the object returned by the parent resolver.
interview.followUp: How can a nested resolver fetch related data? It can use an identifier from the parent object and access a repository or database through context.

interview.question: Can resolvers be asynchronous?
interview.answer: Resolvers may execute asynchronously, so they can obtain data from remote services or databases before returning a value. GraphQL continues completing the result once the resolver's value is available.
interview.followUp: What happens when the value is an object? GraphQL applies the requested selection set recursively until leaf scalar values are reached.

keyPoints: A schema field is backed by server code that determines the data returned for that field.
GraphQL begins field execution at the root operation type selected by the operation.
GraphQL invokes the matching resolver to produce the field's next value.
Object results are expanded by resolving the nested fields requested by the client.
A resolver may return its result asynchronously, supporting data sources that require waiting.
The response map uses the requested field name, or its alias when one is present.
gotchas: A resolver can fail during execution, producing a field error and potentially only partial data in the response.

findBreakingChanges.summary: findBreakingChanges compares a current GraphQL schema with a proposed schema. Use it in CI to detect breaking changes before a pull request is merged.
findBreakingChanges.explanation: The function compares two GraphQLSchema objects and returns detected breaking changes. A CI job can run it for every pull request and stop the build when the result is not empty. The schemas must be built first; raw SDL text is not accepted directly.

parameters.name: currentSchema
parameters.description: The current GraphQLSchema object.

parameters.name: proposedSchema
parameters.description: The proposed GraphQLSchema object.

findBreakingChanges.returns: An array of detected breaking changes. An empty array means no breaking changes were detected.

example.explanation: Build two schemas, compare them, and fail the process when breaking changes are found.

useCases.title: Block breaking changes in CI
useCases.scenario: A pull request changes the schema.

useCases.title: List changes for approval
useCases.scenario: A team needs to review an API change.

useCases.title: Check safe evolution
useCases.scenario: A schema is released incrementally.

interview.question: What does findBreakingChanges do?
interview.answer: findBreakingChanges compares a current schema with a proposed schema and reports breaking changes. A CI check can fail the build when the returned list has items.
interview.followUp: Why is comparing schemas alone incomplete? A schema diff shows possible impact, but production query logs show whether clients actually use the changed field.

interview.question: What input does the function require?
interview.answer: Both inputs must be GraphQLSchema objects. The example creates them with buildSchema before calling the function.
interview.followUp: What should happen when the function finds changes? Print each change, fail CI, and require an explicit review before merging.

interview.question: How should this check be used in CI?
interview.answer: Run the check on every pull request. Store the schema in version control and compare the proposed schema with the current one.
interview.followUp: How can teams improve impact analysis? Combine schema comparison with real client-query usage and performance data.

keyPoints: Automated checks find breaking schema changes before deployment.
Run the comparison for every pull request.
Fail the build when breaking changes are detected.
Keep schema files under version control so proposed and current versions can be compared.
Record why an approved breaking change is needed in the commit message.
A broader schema-diff tool can also detect dangerous changes and connect with CI.
gotchas: Pass schema objects created with buildSchema(), not SDL strings.
Schema differences alone do not show whether real clients use the changed fields. Check query traffic too.
Breaking-change pull requests should need explicit approval before merging.

formatError.summary: GraphQL uses a top-level errors array for exceptional failures. Expected domain failures should be modeled as fields in the schema so clients can discover them.
formatError.explanation: GraphQL reports exceptional failures in a top-level errors array. For expected domain failures, define errors as fields in the schema so clients can discover and handle them as data.
formatError.returns: A GraphQL response can report exceptional failures in errors, or expected domain failures in data fields.

example.title: Top-level GraphQL error
example.explanation: Return exceptional failures in the top-level errors array. The response can also include an error code in extensions.

useCases.title: Report infrastructure failures
useCases.scenario: A database or service failure prevents normal execution.

useCases.title: Return domain errors as data
useCases.scenario: A mutation is rejected because of a known business rule.

useCases.title: Make errors discoverable
useCases.scenario: A client needs to handle known failure states without guessing response formats.

interview.question: When should GraphQL use the top-level errors array?
interview.answer: Use the top-level errors array for infrastructure and system failures, such as a database connection failure. Use errors-as-data for expected, domain-specific failures.
interview.followUp: How should a client discover domain failures? The schema should expose them as fields, allowing clients to query and handle them explicitly.

interview.question: What does errors-as-data mean?
interview.answer: Errors-as-data puts expected failure information in the response data through fields defined by the schema. This makes those states discoverable to clients before they send a request.
interview.followUp: Why is schema discoverability useful? Clients can inspect the fields and choose how to render or recover from known domain outcomes.

interview.question: What information can a top-level GraphQL error contain?
interview.answer: A response for an exceptional failure can contain null data and an errors array. Each error can include a message and an extensions object with an application error code.
interview.followUp: What should an implementation do with the code? It should use a consistent code value, such as INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, so clients can classify the failure.

keyPoints: GraphQL supports both top-level errors and errors-as-data.
Use the top-level errors array for system or infrastructure failures.
Represent expected business failures as fields in the schema.
Choosing the matching error style makes client behavior easier to understand.
Schema fields let clients discover expected error states.
gotchas: Do not use the top-level errors array for expected business outcomes. Model those outcomes as fields in the schema.

fragment.summary: GraphQL fragments are reusable field selections that can be spread into queries. Named fragments support composition, while inline fragments select fields for a concrete type returned through an interface or union.
fragment.explanation: A named fragment packages a reusable set of fields for a particular object, interface, or union type. Place it in a query with the spread syntax (`...FragmentName`); the server applies its selection fields at that location. Inline fragments provide type-specific fields when a field returns an interface or union.

useCases.title: Compose component data requirements
useCases.scenario: Several UI components need different parts of one resource in a single request.

useCases.title: Reuse repeated selections
useCases.scenario: The same group of fields appears in multiple operations.

useCases.title: Select union or interface fields
useCases.scenario: A response field may contain multiple concrete object types.

interview.question: What problem do GraphQL fragments solve?
interview.answer: A fragment is a reusable selection set. A named fragment declares its type condition and is inserted with a fragment spread, so repeated field selections can be shared across queries or components.
interview.followUp: How do you query a union-specific field? Use an inline fragment with the concrete object type as its type condition, then select that type's fields inside it.

interview.question: How is a named fragment declared and used?
interview.answer: The declaration uses `fragment Name on Type`, followed by a selection set. The fragment is included with `...Name` wherever that selection is needed.
interview.followUp: Can a fragment be nested? Yes. A fragment can spread another fragment, allowing larger selections to be composed from smaller reusable selections.

interview.question: When should you use an inline fragment?
interview.answer: Inline fragments are needed when a field returns an interface or union and the requested field belongs to a concrete implementing object. The type condition makes the concrete type explicit.
interview.followUp: What happens when the runtime value is a different member of the union? Fields inside the fragment are returned only when the runtime object matches the fragment's type condition.

keyPoints: Fragments are named, reusable units for grouping fields that belong together.
A fragment is spread into a query to reuse its complete field selection at that location.
Fragments help divide complex data requirements into smaller selections, which can then be composed.
Client components can define separate fragments and combine them into one initial request.
Use inline fragments when the selected field returns an interface or union.
An inline fragment exposes fields defined only by a concrete runtime type.

getIntrospectionQuery.summary: `getIntrospectionQuery` returns a standard GraphQL query string that asks an endpoint for schema metadata. Clients can send it to discover the API’s types, fields, descriptions, and other introspection information.
getIntrospectionQuery.explanation: `getIntrospectionQuery` creates a GraphQL query document that requests schema metadata through the introspection system. A client can send the resulting string to an endpoint and use the response with GraphQL tooling, such as schema construction or code generation.
getIntrospectionQuery.returns: A GraphQL query string for retrieving schema information through introspection.

useCases.title: Power GraphQL tooling
useCases.scenario: Development tools need server metadata to provide autocomplete, validation, documentation, or schema exploration.

useCases.title: Generate client artifacts
useCases.scenario: A build step needs server schema data to construct a client schema or generate typed artifacts.

interview.question: What does `getIntrospectionQuery` do?
interview.answer: It generates a standard GraphQL introspection query as a string. That query asks the server for schema information, including types, fields, and descriptions, through the introspection system.
interview.followUp: What server field does the query ultimately use? The schema is exposed through the `__schema` field on the query root, with related metadata available through introspection types.

interview.question: How is the generated query used?
interview.answer: The returned query can be posted to a GraphQL endpoint like any other query. Its response contains schema metadata that client-side tools can inspect or convert into a usable schema representation.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful for tooling? Introspection queries help power GraphQL development tools by exposing the API’s supported schema features.

interview.question: What deployment limitation should you consider?
interview.answer: Introspection is not guaranteed to be available in every deployment. Some first-party GraphQL APIs disable introspection outside development, so an introspection-based client must handle rejection or use another schema distribution approach.
interview.followUp: Does disabling introspection fully hide the schema? No; the documentation describes it as security through obscurity and recommends broader controls such as trusted documents and authorization.

keyPoints: The function produces a query for GraphQL’s built-in schema-introspection mechanism.
Generated introspection documents are commonly useful to tooling that analyzes or presents a schema.
The query can retrieve the schema through the `__schema` field on the query root.
The returned data can describe schema elements rather than application records.
The standard query covers broad metadata, while GraphQL’s introspection system supports additional schema details.
gotchas: The generated document is intended for schema discovery, not ordinary application data fetching.

gql.summary: GraphQL is an API query language and a server runtime. A schema defines the available data and types, and the server validates and executes client requests.
gql.explanation: GraphQL uses a schema to describe available data and operations. A client sends a query, and the server validates it against that schema before resolvers execute it and return the requested fields.

example.title: A small GraphQL schema
example.explanation: This schema declares the data shape that clients can request.

useCases.scenario: A client needs different fields on different screens.

useCases.title: Use existing data sources
useCases.scenario: An API combines data from application services and storage systems.

useCases.title: Validate API operations
useCases.scenario: A team wants requests checked against a defined contract.

interview.question: What is GraphQL?
interview.answer: GraphQL is a query language for APIs and a server-side runtime. It uses a type system defined by the API author, and it can work with existing code and data.
interview.followUp: Does GraphQL require a specific database? No. It is independent of the storage engine; resolvers connect fields to the data sources.

interview.question: Why is the schema important?
interview.answer: The schema defines the shape of the data that clients can request. It also provides the types used to check whether a query is valid before execution.
interview.followUp: What happens after validation? The server executes the request, using resolvers to produce the fields in the response.

interview.question: Does GraphQL replace a database?
interview.answer: GraphQL is not tied to a database or storage engine. A GraphQL service can use existing application code and data sources behind its schema.
interview.followUp: What does the server runtime do? It validates incoming operations and executes them against the schema to create a response.

keyPoints: Clients use GraphQL to describe the data they want from an API.
The server runs operations using the schema's type system.
GraphQL has an open specification that multiple programming languages implement.
Resolvers can connect GraphQL fields to application code and current data sources.
gotchas: GraphQL does not require a particular database. The server connects the schema to existing code and data.
GraphQL is more than a query format. A server runtime executes requests using the types defined by the schema.

graphql.summary: GraphQL is an API query language and server runtime based on a schema-defined type system. Clients request the fields they need, and the service validates and executes those selections.
graphql.explanation: GraphQL lets a client send a query shaped like the data it needs. The service validates that query against its schema, executes the corresponding field functions, and returns data matching the requested selection set.

useCases.scenario: A client needs a response containing only a subset of an object's fields.

interview.question: What is GraphQL?
interview.answer: GraphQL is a query language for an API plus a server-side runtime. The runtime executes client queries using a type system defined by the service.
interview.followUp: How does a service handle an invalid field? It validates the query against the schema before running the field functions, so an invalid selection is rejected before normal execution.

interview.question: How is a GraphQL service defined?
interview.answer: A service is built by defining types and fields, then supplying a function for each field that returns its data. Those functions can obtain data from the service's underlying sources.
interview.followUp: Can GraphQL require a particular database? No. The schema describes the API interface, while field functions can obtain data from varied underlying sources.

interview.question: How does a GraphQL query differ from a fixed endpoint response?
interview.answer: Clients select the fields they need, and the response follows that selection's shape. This lets one request retrieve nested data without requiring the client to know how the server sources it.
interview.followUp: Why is schema validation useful? It ensures requested selections match the service's declared capabilities before execution begins.

keyPoints: GraphQL combines a client query language with server-side execution governed by a declared type system.
The schema is formed from types and fields that describe the data clients may request.
Each field has execution logic responsible for producing its requested value.
Query structure can directly represent the shape of the result the client wants.
A client can request only selected data and receive it in the corresponding shape through one request.
gotchas: A query cannot request types or fields that the schema does not define; validation happens before execution.
Clients should depend on the GraphQL schema rather than the implementation or storage systems behind individual fields.

GraphQLArgument.summary: GraphQL arguments are named inputs declared by fields or directives. They can be optional or required, may have defaults, and must use input types.
GraphQLArgument.explanation: A GraphQL argument is a named input supplied to a field or directive to influence its result or behavior. Its schema definition specifies an input type and may mark the value as required or provide a default.

example.title: Named field arguments
example.explanation: A query supplies named arguments directly and factors dynamic values into variables.

useCases.title: Customize field results
useCases.scenario: A field needs client-provided criteria such as an identifier, filter, or unit.

useCases.title: Provide defaults
useCases.scenario: A schema offers a sensible behavior when callers omit a nonessential option.

useCases.title: Use variables
useCases.scenario: A query needs dynamic values supplied separately from its document.

interview.question: What is a GraphQL argument?
interview.answer: Arguments are named inputs attached to fields or directives. A field can define zero or more of them, and each argument can alter the field's returned result.
interview.followUp: Why are named arguments useful? They let a field accept several values without depending on positional ordering, so adding or rearranging arguments remains clearer and less error-prone.

interview.question: How do required, optional, and defaulted arguments differ?
interview.answer: An argument is required when its type is non-null; otherwise it is optional. An optional argument may define a default value that is used when the client omits it.
interview.followUp: What happens when a non-null argument is omitted? Validation rejects the operation because the required argument has no supplied value.

interview.question: How are argument values supplied in a query?
interview.answer: Arguments must use input types. GraphQL fields may receive arguments at every nesting level, and variables provide a separate dictionary for dynamic argument values.
interview.followUp: Why use variables instead of embedding dynamic values? Variables separate changing data from the query document and can be supplied through the transport request.

keyPoints: Arguments belong to field definitions, and a field may declare none, one, or many.
A schema gives each argument its own name, such as `unit` on a length field.
Schema authors can choose a fallback value for an optional argument.
Every argument definition declares the input type accepted by that field.
Clients write argument names alongside their values rather than relying on positional slots.
gotchas: Arguments are not positional; changing their order does not change their meaning.
An operation cannot pass an argument that the target field or directive has not declared.
Do not assume an omitted argument is invalid; optional arguments may be absent.

GraphQLBoolean.summary: GraphQL queries read data by selecting specific fields. The response follows the query's shape and contains the requested values.
GraphQLBoolean.explanation: A GraphQL query names the fields it wants from the server. The response follows the same field structure, so the client receives only the requested data. Queries can also use arguments, aliases, fragments, variables, and directives to make field selection more flexible.
GraphQLBoolean.returns: A response containing the requested fields in the same structure as the query.
